name: materialise_decrypted
description: Write decrypted evidence as a durable file under the job's output, from a key the case supplies in a sealed file; the key is nowhere else. Three approved operations, each through a Python reader the pack names in requires/python.txt: `bitlocker_image` (pybde: the volume at a byte `offset` of `source`, unlocked with a recovery password, a password, a startup key file or the clear key, written as a raw image of the unlocked volume), `luks_image` (pyluksde: a LUKS volume unlocked with a password, written as a raw image) and `aescrypt_decrypt` (pyAesCrypt: an AES Crypt container decrypted to a file; the module checks the HMAC before it returns, and the file is named a result only after it has). Selected files out of a volume are NOT provided: the raw image is the durable result and a file system reader works on it afterwards. `key_ref` is a path to a regular file of mode 0600 in the job (a link, pipe, device or directory is refused, at most 4096 bytes, one trailing newline dropped); its content is read by a reader child, a second process of this same file that is given the key file's path (never the key) on its standard input, and handed to the module as an argument in memory. The native modules are never imported or called in the tool's own process: a library that dies of a signal (a SIGSEGV in `unlock` or in a later `read_buffer`), hangs, forks or ignores SIGTERM cannot take the tool down. The tool starts no program but that child (and a first child that only tries the import), so the key is on no command line; it is not in the environment, the answer, a path, a key of the JSON or a file, and a module's exception text is never shown (it may quote the key): only its class is. A call that is not a job run as secret output (SECRET_OUTPUT=1; this manifest's `secret_output: "required"` makes every job of this tool one) is refused as JSON before anything is read, its own stdin included. A module that is not importable answers `unavailable`, naming it, before the key file's bytes are read (the import is tried by a child, and one that dies on import is a `failed` answer, not a crash). A reader that dies of a signal gives `failed` and names the signal, and the `.partial` file is removed (the bytes it had written are not verified). A reader that does not return in a library call is ended at the tool's clock with everything it started (only processes of the tool's own group that it saw, each checked again before it is signalled): `failed` if it had written nothing, otherwise `partial` with the file kept as an unverified `.partial` whose digest is not computed (the provenance file says so). A reader whose report does not match the size of the file is `failed`, never `complete`. Every output is first a file ending in `.partial`, created exclusively with mode 0600 under the job's `materialised/` directory. A key that does not work (`failed`) removes it: nothing is left, and the answer says that this says nothing about another key or protector. A whole result is placed under its final name (`decrypted-<operation>.img` or `.bin`; a name that is taken by other bytes gives the next free one, the same bytes the same name) and `complete` means the reader unlocked or decrypted it and the output was written to the end (a BitLocker or LUKS image: the whole unlocked size; AES Crypt: the module's HMAC check passed). A result that is not whole (the volume ends early, the output budget `max_output_bytes` is reached, the tool's clock runs out, an AES Crypt container cut short, which is told by its length before any plaintext is written) is `partial` and the file is kept as an unverified `.partial`. A stop signal ends with one JSON answer and exit 128 + the signal and leaves the `.partial` file. The provenance of each output is a file of its own beside it (`<output>.provenance.json`, mode 0600): the reader's name and version, the evidence's path, size, offset and sha256 (unless `hash_evidence` is false), the kind of key used and the key reference (the protector's identifier is not reported by the modules), the output's size and sha256 and the integrity checks made (the AES Crypt HMAC, or the first sector of an unlocked volume read for a file system signature: NTFS, exFAT, FAT or a boot signature). The digests are in that file and not in the answer because the shared output check replaces long hexadecimal runs in an answer. The behaviour of the modules is taken from their documented calls (volume().open_file_object, set_recovery_password, set_password, read_startup_key, unlock, get_size, read_buffer; decryptStream) and tested here against stand-in modules and, where it is installed, the real pyAesCrypt; pybde and pyluksde were not run on a real volume in this change. Its own clock (`max_seconds`, 480 by default, at most 540) is below the manifest's timeout. Withholding is by shape, measured on random draws per shape planted in a member name or path (rates, not guarantees). Printed whole in 0 of 1,000 draws: hexadecimal ids of 16, 32 and 64, numbers of 10 digits or more, recovery passwords written with dashes, spaces, dots, underscores, no separator or one to three of any other characters between the groups (an en dash, a comma, a colon, a pipe, a tab), also when the groups are cut at the separators of the path (123456-123456/123456-...), full-width, split by invisible characters, or with one decimal digit glued to the first or last group, AWS access key ids, password= and api_key: assignments, user-info, 4x4 groups of capitals and digits joined by - or ., letters and digits of 8, 9, 12, 16 or 40 characters that hold a capital, a small letter and a digit, and a full-width id. Printed whole in some draws: uniform draws of letters and digits (every character as likely a capital, a small letter or a digit as any other) of 8 characters about 2.5%, of 9 about 2%, of 12 about 1%, of 16 about 0.6%, of 24 at most 0.1% and of 40 none; random lowercase letters and digits of 8 about 7%, of 12 about 2.4%, of 16 about 0.4%; 24 random letters 1.5% to 2.6%; a 16-character base32 id 2.2% to 3.4% (by alphabet); four groups of four lowercase hexadecimal digits joined by underscores 4% to 9% (by how the draws are made); an id of 12 or 16 characters whose letters are half Cyrillic or Greek look-alikes about 1%. NOT recognised, by design, and printed whole: an identifier of 7 characters or fewer, a number of 9 digits or fewer, a lowercase-only run of up to 22 letters (it reads as a word), an all-capital letters-only run of any length, three groups of four or five capitals and digits joined by - or . (a rule for them would also withhold upper-case constants such as OpenSSL manual page names), a recovery password cut by anything other than a separator or with a letter in it or glued to it (the groups then show), a ten-digit number written 3-3-4, an e-mail-like lowercase string, and a secret of any other shape; a file whose secrets matter is read in a job run with secret_output: true. What the rule is given is bounded: a string of more than 4096 characters (as written or after folding), a path of more than 8192, or a string with a / and a run of more than 256 name characters is withheld whole as '<text too long to judge withheld>' and not judged (the slowest string inside the bound that a search found took 0.13 CPU s). The output check, which reads every printed string once more, is narrower than the rule: with the rule removed it replaces recovery passwords (full-width ones too), AWS ids, password= values, PEM headers, user-info, hexadecimal of 16 digits or more and runs of 24 or more characters that flip between letters and digits, and it lets through numbers of 10 to 20 digits, ids of up to 23 characters, some base64 (about one in five of 32 bytes), every recovery password whose groups are joined by anything but a hyphen, underscore, dot, space or nothing, and every recovery password cut over the components of a path (the first layer alone holds those). The rule also changes names that are not secrets: of the file names of a documents tree 6.9% have a part withheld (10-digit timestamps, UUIDs) and 0.6% of its directories, of an application tree 16% and 3.1% (a word with a digit inside, such as libmp3lame, is withheld in part). A name, a path, a URL or a message that quotes a credential is withheld with the identifier-shaped strings, from version 2: a value given to a password, token, secret or cookie name (password=..., Pwd=..., a Cookie header), a Name/Value pair in text whose Name is a credential (a number, an array or a long Value too, and the NewValue after an OldValue), a -Password style switch, the argument of ConvertTo-SecureString, curl -u user:pass, mysql -uUSER -pSECRET, a bcrypt hash and the known token families; the text is replaced by a marker that holds only its length. Before, only identifier-shaped strings (tokens, key ids, user-info) were withheld, so these were printed. Known gaps: a pair whose Value is an array nested in another or longer than 4,096 characters, a crypt hash that is not bcrypt, and a secret that has neither a credential name nor a token shape.

source.description: The evidence file: a disk or partition image holding the volume (bitlocker_image, luks_image) or an AES Crypt container; a link, pipe or device is refused

key_ref.description: A path to a regular file of mode 0600 in the job holding the key (a recovery password, a password, a startup key file for key_kind startup_key). Not needed for key_kind clear_key. Never a value given inline

key_kind.description: bitlocker_image: recovery_password, password, startup_key or clear_key; luks_image and aescrypt_decrypt: password (the default)

offset.description: Byte offset of the volume within source (default 0); for bitlocker_image and luks_image

max_output_bytes.description: The most decrypted bytes written (default 1 GiB, at most 64 GiB); a larger result is kept as a partial file

hash_evidence.description: Whether the evidence's sha256 is computed for the provenance (default true; the whole file is read once)

max_seconds.description: The tool's own time limit in seconds (default 480, 1 to 540; the manifest's timeout is 600)
